stories.headline: Putin seeks new tax revenue to fund Russia's war as budget deficit swells
stories.title: Putin seeks new tax revenue to fund Russia's war as budget deficit swells
stories.summary: With Russia's invasion of Ukraine intensifying the strain on state finances, President Vladimir Putin is reaching for cash to fund his government and the war, squeezing tax revenue from an economy that's increasingly skewed toward the military - while civilian needs take a back seat. The country's 2027-2029 state budget, which will be taken up Thursday in the rubber-stamp parliament, is accompanied by a string of tax hikes announced after the September parliamentary elections. While last year the Kremlin went for a broad tax increase, raising value-added taxes at the cash register and making more small businesses pay VAT, this cash grab hits a narrower segment: mining companies and better-off citizens with investment income, property sales and bank accounts. The budget deficit this year has swelled beyond forecasts due to lavish military spending and tepid economic growth amid sanctions, high interest rates for non-military companies, labour shortages and Ukrainian strikes on oil ..

article_sentences: Major rivers in the north Andhra districts of Srikakulam, Vizianagaram and Parvathipuram Manyam continued to receive heavy inflows from their catchment areas on Thursday (October 29, 2026), though the weather cleared after Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast on Wednesday.
The Bahuda river received 58,436 cusecs of water after flood water was released from the Baghalati dam in Odisha.
Flood water entered the border town of Ichchapuram and surrounding areas, but the situation is under control, Srikakulam Collector Swapnil Dinakar Pundkar said.
Following heavy inflows into the Vamsadhara, irrigation officials released 56,272 cusecs of water on Thursday.
Officials released 15,450 cusecs of water in the Nagavali river at the old bridge in Srikakulam after two days of continuous inflows.
A special control room has been set up at the Collector’s office (08942-240557) to monitor the flood situation in several parts of the district.
Several low-lying areas of Parvathipuram Manyam district were flooded after the Suvarnamukhi river swelled.
Vizianagaram district received an average of 187.13 mm of rain on October 28, against a normal of about 1.36 mm for the day, according to the Water Resources Department.
Srikakulam district got 131.33 mm and Parvathipuram Manyam 81.80 mm.
In each of the three districts, that one day brought more than three-quarters of all the rain recorded so far in October.
The Nagavali at Srikakulam stood at 10.16 metres at noon on Thursday and was still rising, just 1 cm below its warning level of 10.17 metres, the department’s data showed.
The danger level is 10.8 metres.

article_sentences: With heavy rain and gale under the influence of very severe cyclonic storm Arnab leaving a trail of destruction in Visakhapatnam, the candidates in the fray for the civic body polls in the city have shifted focus from electioneering to relief and restoration work.

The candidates belonging to the ruling alliance and opposition parties, who were busy in hectic campaign in the run-up to the civic body polls scheduled for November 1, visited the affected neighbourhoods to assist the residents and coordinate efforts to restore essential services.

From Tuesday evening, several candidates were seen working in their respective wards, alongside the workers and Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) personnel, to clear choked drains, remove fallen trees, address waterlogging issues and coordinate with the Andhra Pradesh Eastern Power Distribution Company Limited (APEPDCL) to restore power supply.
For many candidates, it was an opportunity to demonstrate their accessibility and responsiveness to ward-level issues at this crucial juncture.
NDA mayoral candidate Mukka Sravani participated in relief and restoration efforts in Akkayyapalem, where fallen electric poles and uprooted trees caused inconvenience to residents.
She alerted the authorities concerned about the damage and coordinated with officials to expedite restoration work.
In Bheemunipatnam, YSRCP Assembly constituency coordinator Botcha Anusha, daughter of YSRCP MLC Botcha Satyanarayana, toured several low-lying areas to assess the impact of the cyclone.
Accompanied by corporator candidates, she visited localities near hillocks and distributed relief material to affected residents.
Several TDP and YSRCP candidates were involved in clearing fallen trees and debris in China Waltair on Tuesday night.
Their teams remained on the ground as residents struggled to navigate roads blocked by fallen trees.
In One Town, several YSRCP corporator candidates took part in efforts to clear fallen electric poles and facilitate the restoration of drinking water supplies.
They visited rehabilitation centres to check on the condition of residents evacuated from vulnerable localities and ensure that basic amenities were available.

article_sentences: Guntur district recorded an average rainfall of 41 mm as on 9 a.m., Wednesday, with Duggirala mandal receiving the highest rainfall of 77.8 mm, followed by Tadepalle at 71.2 mm and Chebrole at 70 mm, amid the impact of cyclone Arnab.

According to the daily rainfall statistics, Mangalagiri and Kollipara received 66.6 mm each, Tenali 63.8 mm, Pedakakani 50.8 mm, Guntur East 38.4 mm, Guntur West 38.2 mm, Tadikonda 36 mm, Thullur 31.8 mm, Ponnur 24.5 mm, Kakumanu 21.6 mm, Medikonduru 18.6 mm, Vatticherukuru 17.4 mm, Pedanandipadu 16.2 mm, Prathipadu 15.6 mm and Phirangipuram 12.4 mm.
District Collector C.M. Saikanth Varma directed officials to remain at the field level and maintain heightened vigilance throughout Wednesday in view of the cyclone and continuing rainfall.

During a teleconference with officials, the Collector instructed them to inspect low-lying areas, assess the situation and ensure uninterrupted road connectivity, noting that strong winds were prevailing and stressing the need for prompt action to address emerging problems.

Stating that a tree that had fallen at Emani village in Duggirala mandal had been removed, Mr. Varma instructed Roads and Buildings and Panchayat Raj engineers to continuously monitor road conditions and take immediate remedial measures.
Water Resources Department engineers were directed to monitor water flows at Prakasam Barrage and other channels.
Schools and colleges in the district were declared closed for the day as a precautionary measure.
The Collector said Yanadi families had already been shifted to rehabilitation centres.
He instructed officials to provide quality food to the families and milk to children.
He directed all departments to submit regular situation reports and remain fully alert throughout the day.
He also cautioned people against venturing near streams, rivulets, tanks and rivers during the adverse weather conditions.

stories.title: Supreme Court Refuses To Entertain Challenge To Casual Vacancy Election In Punjab &Haryana Bar Council
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 29) declined to entertain a petition filed by an advocate challenging the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana's decision to conduct an election to fill up the casual vacancy which arose following the recommendation for the elevation of an elected member as a Judge of the High Court.
A bench comprising Justice Vikram Nath, Justice Sandeep Mehta and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh heard the petition filed by advocate Chetan Verma.

Verma had approached the Supreme Court challenging an October 9 order passed by Election Tribunal No. 2 at New Delhi, which rejected his plea seeking to be declared a member of the Bar Council against a vacancy that arose after Minderjeet Yadav, an elected member, was elevated as a judge of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
The appeal was filed under Section 38 of the Advocates Act, 1961.
Verma had contested the Bar Council of Punjab and Haryana elections held in March 2026.
He claimed that he had secured the highest number of votes among the unsuccessful candidates and had not been eliminated during the vote-counting process.
Following the Collegium's recommendation for Yadav's elevation to the High Court, Verma claimed that he was entitled to fill the resulting vacancy.
He argued that the election process had not been fully completed when the vacancy arose.
However, the Election Tribunal rejected his claim, holding that the vacancy was a casual vacancy governed by Rules 45 and 46 of the applicable rules.
It observed that the rules did not provide for the automatic induction of the highest unsuccessful candidate to fill such a vacancy.

The Tribunal held that a casual vacancy among the elected members of the Bar Council had to be filled in accordance with the prescribed procedure, which provides for an election among eligible advocates.
The Tribunal also vacated its interim order restraining the Bar Council from filling the vacancy, permitting it to proceed in accordance with law and the directions issued by the Supreme Court.

stories.headline: The 2026 Midterms
stories.title: The 2026 Midterms
stories.summary: What does democracy mean when a government’s decisions are felt far beyond its borders, in bombed neighbourhoods, displaced families, rising fuel prices and weakened international restraints on power? As Americans approach the 3 November 2026 midterm elections, this question reaches the heart of electoral accountability: will voters judge the Trump administration only by domestic prices and partisan loyalties, or also by the human consequences of American power abroad? A Pew Research Center survey published on 8 October found that 84 per cent of registered voters considered the economy very important to their vote; 73 per cent said the future of democracy mattered greatly, while 57 per cent named foreign policy. These priorities are intertwined. Military escalation can unsettle energy markets and household budgets, while spending choices determine what governments fund at home and abroad. The question is whether voters will connect these consequences, or debate each in isolation. Iran is the most immediate test. The conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes in February, has become a strategic gamble and a domestic political liability. Pew’s survey of September 28–October 4 found that 65 per cent of Americans disapproved of President Donald Trump’s handling of US military action against Iran, while 33 per cent approved. Only 16 per cent were very or extremely confident that the administration would achieve its goals; 77 per cent expected the conflict to last at least another six months. These figures raise questions about the war’s objectives, civilian protection, regional escalation and the absence of a credible political endgame. Reports that Trump would avoid attacking Iran before the midterms while negotiations continue sharpen the dilemma. If military decisions are adjusted around an electoral calendar, voters can ask whether strategy is being driven by long-term security or short-term political calculation. Iran’s government must also be scrutinised for its own conduct and regional actions; criticism of Washington does not require romanticising Tehran. But one state’s abuses do not remove the obligation to assess another state’s use of force under consistent standards: evidence, international law, civilian protection and a realistic path to de-escalation. Uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz affects oil prices, shipping and insurance, transmitting geopolitical risk into household budgets worldwide. A president cannot credibly promise economic stability while treating the consequences of military action as incidental. Voters should ask what measurable outcome would count as success, what the exit strategy is, and who will bear the costs if the conflict expands. Human rights abroad and the question of American consent Iran is only one part of the larger moral and political question. US support for Israel amid the devastation in Gaza, violence in Lebanon, and coercive rhetoric towards other territories raise questions about how consistently Washington applies its stated commitment to human rights. The issue is whether officials investigate credible evidence of civilian harm, scrutinise allies as well as adversaries, and make military assistance conditional on compliance with law. Human rights should not be a vocabulary deployed against geopolitical rivals and abandoned when an ally is involved. Civilian deaths, forced displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access, arbitrary detention and allegations of collective punishment require serious, independent examination wherever they occur. The same standard should apply to US policy, including the foreseeable consequences of arms transfers, sanctions, military operations and security partnerships. Where legal findings remain contested or facts incomplete, analysis must say so. Uncertainty is not a reason for silence, but neither is it a licence to present allegations as adjudicated facts. At home, immigration enforcement, detention and deportation practices have prompted concerns about due process, family separation and the treatment of vulnerable people. Governments may enforce borders and pursue security objectives; they remain bound by constitutional protections and legal obligations. The key questions are whether safeguards work, whether allegations of abuse are independently investigated, and whether affected people have meaningful access to remedies. It would be revealing to discover whether American voters approve or disapprove of human rights violations attributed to the Trump administration—or regard them as secondary to economic interests, immigration control or national security. Existing polling indicates broad disapproval of Trump’s handling of Iran, but it does not establish whether voters would punish the administration electorally for civilian harm, due-process violations or the conduct of US-backed forces. A rigorous poll would ask about specific actions, distinguish verified findings from allegations, and test whether attitudes change when respondents learn about civilian consequences and legal obligations. It would examine partisan differences without assuming party identity determines every moral judgment. The answers could reveal whether human rights function as a genuine democratic standard or are invoked selectively to reinforce prior loyalties. Political theory helps frame the issue. Robert Dahl’s account of polyarchy emphasises meaningful competition and opportunities to contest power; Jürgen Habermas’s public sphere depends on access to information and open debate. Elections confer authority, but they cannot make that authority a blank cheque. A vote for a party cannot be read as approval of every action by its leaders. Those actions must remain open to scrutiny between elections as well as during them. Beyond November: Accountability, not just party victory The midterms will be counted in seats, margins and turnout. Their deeper meaning will depend on whether Congress can investigate executive decisions, scrutinise military spending, demand legal justifications and make oversight more than partisan theatre. The test is whether institutions apply consistent standards regardless of who occupies the White House. The economy remains central. Pew found that 84 per cent of registered voters ranked it as very important to their midterm vote, while foreign policy mattered to 57 per cent. The Iran conflict may influence voters partly through petrol prices and economic insecurity. Yet a democracy that judges war only by the price at the pump adopts an impoverished moral calculus: civilian lives abroad matter independently of whether conflict raises costs at home. Human-rights arguments, meanwhile, are weakened when they ignore the security fears and political pressures shaping public opinion. Voters should demand answers from candidates. What are the legal grounds and strategic objectives for military action? What safeguards govern arms transfers and cooperation with foreign forces? How are allegations of civilian harm investigated? What limits should apply to detention, deportation and executive power? Will representatives support independent oversight even when scrutiny embarrasses their own party? These questions do not prescribe a particular electoral choice; they establish minimum standards for democratic accountability. Journalists and universities must distinguish established facts, credible allegations and political claims. The language of “human rights violations” should be used seriously, with attention to evidence and legal standards, not merely as a rhetorical weapon. But demands for perfect certainty must not become an excuse to ignore credible evidence or avoid scrutiny of powerful governments. Critical analysis requires both moral clarity and factual discipline. The 2026 midterms will not deliver a definitive verdict on every US action in Iran, Gaza, Lebanon or elsewhere. Nor can one election resolve the tension between national interest and universal rights. But it offers a revealing test: do Americans want their representatives to scrutinise the human consequences of power, including when those consequences are borne by people outside the United States? If voters demand transparency, legality and accountability, the ballot can restrain executive power. If they treat rights as expendable whenever partisan loyalty or national advantage is invoked, electoral consent risks becoming permission without limits. Democracy is measured not only by who wins office, but by what citizens insist their government must never do without explanation. The author is an independent researcher based in Kashmir.

stories.headline: Reading the mountain before we build on it
stories.title: Reading the mountain before we build on it
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir is often described in poetry, but its mountains also speak in a language of numbers. One recent set of numbers deserves the attention of every planner, engineer, farmer and traveller who cares for this land. In August 2026, the journal Scientific Reports, part of Nature Portfolio, published a study on landslide risk in our region. The paper is titled GIS based multi criteria landslide susceptibility assessment in the northwestern Himalaya, Jammu and Kashmir, India. It was led by Prof Avtar Singh Jasrotia and researchers from the Department of Geology at the University of Jammu, and it appeared on August 28. The study mapped 42,950.43 square kilometres of mountainous terrain across Jammu and Kashmir. The researchers looked at slope, rock type, rainfall, rivers, land use and the distance of each place from roads, and then asked a simple question. Where is the ground most likely to give way? The answer was clear. About 28.08 per cent of the mapped area, or roughly 12,062 square kilometres, falls in the high or very high landslide susceptibility zones. In plain words, more than one fourth of the mapped land needs extra care before any digging or building begins. Proximity to roads was found among the important variables in the modelling, which means that slopes disturbed by road construction deserve special attention. It is important to read this finding in the right spirit. It does not say that roads are bad. A road is a lifeline in the mountains. It carries the patient to the hospital, the child to school and the apple to the market. The study only tells us that the hill has its own temperament, and that good planning works best when it begins with a good map. The same spirit was visible at the 13th Sustainable Mountain Development Summit, held at the Shalimar campus of SKUAST Kashmir on October 12, 2026. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah spoke there about making Jammu and Kashmir the first Himalayan region with a full Mountain Development Policy. The talk included scientific road building, safe waste handling at new tourist places and respect for the carrying limits of fragile slopes. A policy of this kind grows stronger when it rests on evidence, and the new landslide map offers exactly that. Many hands have been working on this subject. Last year, a study on landslides was completed with the contribution of engineers and assistant professors of Geology and Geography, and the writer was glad to be one of its authors. A related paper on landslide risk along the national highways of Jammu and Kashmir was presented at a conference in New Zealand on February 3 and 4, 2026. These are modest efforts, meant as one more brick in a wall of knowledge that many scholars are building together. Some years ago, the Environment Committee of the Legislative Council was headed by this writer. The committee met forest officers, universities and climate experts, including some from Hyderabad, and held awareness programmes at nearly a dozen district headquarters. A document for the region was prepared. Its recommendations did not turn into policy, and perhaps a little more energy from the chair would have helped. The lesson is a happy one all the same. Good reports are never wasted, and the new policy could begin by reading them afresh alongside the new landslide map. Weather adds urgency. Rain and snow are behaving differently now, and dry springs, cloudbursts and flash floods are becoming more common. Roads, tunnels, hotels and homes can all be checked against hazard maps before approval. A geological check before work, good drainage and safe dumping of soil will keep slopes steady and families safe. The economy of the region also has a stake in this. Horticulture earns about ₹10,000 crore every year, supports around 35 lakh people and adds about 6 to 7 per cent to the region’s GDP, according to the NITI Aayog roadmap. Land in Kashmir is limited, and once an orchard becomes concrete it does not come back. Compact towns and sensible tall buildings can save farmland, as long as water supply, sewage and earthquake safety are checked first. Tourism, too, can grow with the mountains and not against them. It feeds hoteliers, drivers, guides, artisans and pony handlers, and it deserves full support. New places beyond Gulmarg, Pahalgam and Sonamarg can share the benefits more widely. A place should be ready before guests arrive, with working sewage treatment, waste disposal, water and parking. A published study of how many visitors a place can comfortably take, reviewed from time to time, would be a big help. All these threads need one hand to hold them. Roads, forests, tourism, farming, towns and disaster management work best under a common plan. That plan can have clear targets, open data, a voice for villagers and farmers and a yearly report card that everyone can read. The choice before us is not between development and nature. It is between development that understands the mountain from the beginning and development that learns about it later. With the new policy, the new research and the goodwill of many institutions, Jammu and Kashmir has a fine chance to choose the first path. If it does, the results will show in stable slopes, green orchards, clean rivers and secure livelihoods. Caring for our mountains is not just a nice idea. It is a matter of safety, income and our future. Let us keep learning from the hills, and from each other. Dr S Bashir Ahmad Veeri is a serving legislator from South Kashmir and contributes occasionally on public policy and governance.

stories.title: Supreme Court Refuses Mahua Moitra's Plea To Mandate Disclosure Of Ultimate Beneficial Owners Of AIFs & FPIs
stories.summary: The Court observed that in the absence of an existing legal framework, it cannot issue such a direction.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Court observed that in the absence of an existing legal framework, it cannot issue such a direction.

The Supreme Court on Thursday declined to issue a direction to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to mandate full public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners (last natural persons) and portfolios of Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) and their intermediaries in India.

Citing the lack of an existing legal or regulatory framework, the bench comprising Justice BV Nagarathna, Justice R Mahadevan and Justice DK Upadhyaya disposed of the writ petition filed by Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra.

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, for the petitioner, argued that the lack of public disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners of these investment vehicles had created opacity in the stock market and enabled potential manipulation.
Bhushan submitted that large sums of money were being invested in Indian companies through foreign entities, but the identity of the actual investors remained unknown.
“These people who are investing into our companies through foreign entities, we don't know who they are and whether they are violating SEBI regulations.
Today there is a lot of suspicion that stock markets are being manipulated by these companies which are investing huge sums,” he said.

He contended that the requirement of disclosing the ultimate beneficial owner, which existed earlier, was given up in 2018, after which entities were only required to comply with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).

Referring to the observations of the expert committee appointed by the Supreme Court in the Adani-Hindenburg case, Bhushan argued that the removal of the disclosure requirement had weakened the regulatory framework.
He said: “Let's say shares of a company are going up very rapidly and very steeply.

Then some stock broker tells the retail investor that the share is going up, why don't you put money into this share… This person does not know that the reason the share price is going up is because the promoters of that very company are buying the shares through an AIF or an FPI, thereby boosting the share price.
Then he will not buy the share.”

stories.title: Supreme Court says it has not decided on legality of ‘logical discrepancy’ in SIR
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court, on October 28, clarified that it has not yet ruled on the legality of the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) use of the ‘logical discrepancy’ category during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The court said it had allowed the category in West Bengal only as an interim measure, and that its earlier ruling on the Bihar SIR had not settled the issue.

A three-judge bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana made the observations while hearing petitions challenging aspects of the ongoing SIR in Delhi.

The petitions, filed by RTI activist Anjali Bhardwaj and another individual, raise concerns about the transparency of notices issued to voters and the requirement for those excluded from the draft electoral rolls to apply afresh for inclusion.

Justice Bagchi said the Bihar judgement could not be treated as a final determination of every issue arising from the SIR exercise, since the ECI had not used the logical discrepancy category in Bihar.
The court had subsequently permitted its use in West Bengal as an interim arrangement, but had not ruled on its legality.
“Bihar SIR is not a binding precedent.
There, the ECI had not undertaken Logical Discrepancy as a category.
We have permitted you in Bengal as an interim arrangement.
We have not finally adjudicated on the legality of Logical Discrepancy,” Justice Bagchi said.
The judge also cautioned against treating oral observations made during hearings as conclusive decisions, particularly in sensitive matters.
He said the court did not want to make further comments that could be quoted out of context as though every question had already been decided.

stories.headline: Supreme Court's Requests To Courts Or Tribunals Must Be Treated As Directions : Supreme Court
stories.title: Supreme Court's Requests To Courts Or Tribunals Must Be Treated As Directions : Supreme Court
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court has observed that any request made by it to a court or tribunal must be construed as a direction, warning that non-compliance with such directions would be viewed seriously.

A bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice K. Vinod Chandran has expressed displeasure over the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal's (NCLAT) failure to hear a company appeal despite an earlier order requesting it to do so.
“When the Supreme Court makes a request to any Court or Tribunal, it has to be construed as a direction and not just a request.”, the Court observed.

The Court was hearing a miscellaneous application, where in its earlier order, the Court had requested the NCLAT to ensure that the matter was heard on July 23, considering that the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) had reserved its order on an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).
However, on Tuesday (October 27), the applicant's counsel informed the Court that the NCLAT had not heard the matter.
In the meantime, the NCLT had pronounced its order admitting the Section 7 IBC application.

Expressing concern over the development, the Court stated that its earlier request had been made out of deference to the NCLAT's position and to ensure that the judicial office held by its members was not belittled.
The Court clarified that although it may make an earnest request in the expectation that a court or tribunal would act accordingly, such a request must be treated as a direction.

“If there is any request made by the Supreme Court to any Court or Tribunal, the same shall be treated as a direction and non-compliance of such direction shall be looked into very seriously.”, the Court said.
As a result, the notice was issued, and an explanation was sought from the NCLAT as to why the matter had not been heard despite its earlier order.

stories.title: IMD update: Fresh depression alert as Arnab brings heavy rain to Chhattisgarh, UP, MP
stories.summary: Heavy rain forecast also for eastern Uttar Pradesh and eastern Madhya Pradesh as IMD taps fresh ‘low’ over South Andaman Sea to become a depression in the next two days
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Barely two mornings after very severe cyclone Arnab made landfall, the Bay of Bengal is stirring again.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has identified a fresh low-pressure area over the South Andaman Sea, which could intensify into a depression within the next two days as a back-to-back weather system over the basin.
The new system is taking shape even as Arnab’s remnants continue to unload rain over central India.
The cyclone’s remnant circulation lay as a depression over south Chhattisgarh and adjoining south Odisha this Thursday morning, centred about 20 km west of Jagdalpur in Chhattisgarh.
During the 12 hours ending at 5.30 am on Thursday, Odisha, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam recorded heavy to very heavy rainfall.
Gopalpur in Odisha and Machilipatnam in Andhra Pradesh received 9 cm each; Balasore, Paradip Port, Tuni and Amaravati in Andhra Pradesh recorded 7 cm each.
Keonjhar and Visakhapatnam received 6 cm each, while Jharsuguda recorded 5 cm.
The IMD has forecast isolated very heavy rainfall over East Uttar Pradesh on Thursday, with isolated heavy to very heavy rain likely over East Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.
East Uttar Pradesh could see isolated heavy rainfall on Friday as well.
The remnant depression from Arnab is expected to track nearly northwards and weaken into a well-marked low-pressure area by Thursday evening.
But as Arnab’s remnants gradually lose steam over land, the Bay is already preparing for another round of activity.
The speed with which a fresh ‘low’ has emerged after a very severe cyclone is noteworthy.

New York: India has reiterated its opposition to legislation that "adversely affects the sovereignty" of other states while backing a United Nations General Assembly resolution calling for an end to the long-running US economic embargo against Cuba.

Addressing the Assembly ahead of the ballot, Soumya Nair, a counsellor at India’s Permanent Mission to the UN, stated that New Delhi supports the global body's call urging member states to reject “laws and regulations with extraterritorial effects that adversely affect the sovereignty of other states and the progress and prosperity of their peoples”.

She stressed, “India reiterates the Assembly’s call to all states to refrain from promulgating and applying, and to repeal and invalidate such laws and measures in conformity with their obligations under the Charter of the United Nations and International Law”.
The resolution was adopted with 130 votes in favour, 17 against, and 25 abstentions.

The vote occurred following a tense confrontation on the Assembly floor on Tuesday, during which Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla approached the lectern to challenge US Permanent Representative Mike Waltz mid-address.
In response to the disruption, Assembly President Khalilur Rahman briefly halted proceedings to restore order.

Diplomatic friction escalated further on Wednesday when the United States expelled Richard Tur de la Concepción, First Secretary at the Cuban mission, following allegations that he physically confronted an American diplomat during Tuesday's incident, according to Ambassador Waltz.

Asserting a strict posture, Waltz declared, “If you lay a hand on an American diplomat in this body, there will be consequences,” adding, “That so-called diplomat today will be put on a plane back to Havana.”
The initial altercation occurred while Waltz was speaking to the General Assembly regarding alleged corruption within Cuba’s ruling leadership.

Commenting on the event, Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General António Guterres, criticised the breach of protocol during a Wednesday news briefing, stating, “We expect every delegation to respect the decorum of the General Assembly’s hall and to respect the rules and procedures of the General Assembly.”
He added that UN Safety and Security officers were deployed in larger numbers and “did a great job in ensuring that the situation did not get out of hand”.
